title: Columbia study recruiting: magnetic brain stimulation to help movement recover after brain tumor surgery
summary: Columbia University is running a single-center, open-label pilot study of image-guided repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) for adults who have movement problems after surgery to remove a brain tumor. Six patients are planned: three with new motor deficits one to two weeks after surgery, who also get physical therapy, and three with persistent deficits up to three years after surgery, with or without physical therapy. Each person gets stimulation once a day for three days in a row, using inhibitory theta burst stimulation over motor areas on the healthy side of the brain and excitatory theta burst stimulation over motor areas on the operated side. The main outcomes are side effects and change in muscle strength on the British Medical Research Council (MRC) scale one week after treatment, with follow-up at 1 week, 1 month, 3 months and 6 months.
quick_read: This small study at Columbia University in New York is testing whether a non-invasive magnetic stimulation treatment can help people regain movement after brain tumor surgery. Magnetic pulses are given through the scalp to the brain areas that control movement, once a day for three days. It is open both to people with new weakness one to two weeks after surgery and to people who still have weakness up to three years later. The main goals are to check safety and whether muscle strength improves, so it is an early step rather than a proven treatment.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few recruiting trials built specifically for weakness caused by brain tumor surgery, and it accepts people with long-standing deficits, not just the first weeks after the operation. It is very small and early, and people with any history of seizures are excluded, which rules out many brain tumor patients.
relevance_reason: Recruiting trial aimed directly at motor deficits after brain tumor surgery, including chronic deficits up to 3 years.
evidence_level: Recruiting pilot trial (single-arm, open-label, 6 participants planned)

trial_status.location: Columbia University Irving Medical Center, New York, NY, USA

title: Four-center analysis of 135 patients: magnetic stimulation plus physiotherapy helped arm weakness after brain tumor surgery
source: Journal of Neuro-Oncology (Charité Berlin, TU Munich, King's College Hospital, MD Anderson)
summary: Researchers pooled two randomized trials and three single-arm studies of brain tumor patients with new or worsened arm weakness after surgery. Patients received low-frequency navigated repetitive TMS over the motor cortex on the healthy side of the brain (to reduce its inhibition of the injured side), or sham stimulation, followed by physiotherapy. Of 135 patients, 51 were in the randomized trials (30 treated, 21 sham). The treated group did better on muscle strength (BMRC) at 7 days and on overall functional status (Karnofsky score) at 7 days and 3 months, with a smaller, uncertain difference on the Fugl-Meyer motor scale. The effect was stronger in patients whose MRI showed a small stroke (ischemia) from surgery, and the authors estimate that about 4 patients need treatment for one to gain at least one strength grade at 3 months.
quick_read: Some people develop new weakness in an arm after brain tumor surgery. This study combined results from hospitals in Germany, the UK and the US, where 135 such patients received either a magnetic stimulation treatment through the scalp or a fake version, followed by physiotherapy. Those who got the real stimulation regained strength and everyday function faster, and the benefit was clearest when surgery had caused a small stroke near the movement areas. It adds to growing evidence that this non-invasive treatment can support rehabilitation, although larger randomized trials are still needed.
why_it_matters: It is the largest pooled dataset so far on TMS for weakness caused specifically by brain tumor surgery, and it focuses on the arm and hand. Only 51 patients were randomized, and the strength advantage at 3 months was not statistically certain, so it supports but does not prove the approach.
relevance_reason: Multicenter human data on a rehab-boosting treatment for arm weakness caused by brain tumor surgery.
evidence_level: Human study (secondary analysis of 2 RCTs and 3 single-arm studies, 135 patients)
date_note: Published online 2025-01-23; print issue April 2025.

title: Randomized trial in glioma surgery patients: stimulating the brain's hand area sped up recovery of strength
summary: Thirty glioma patients with motor deficits after surgery were randomized to high-frequency neuro-navigated repetitive TMS or sham stimulation targeting the hand area (hand knob) of the motor cortex on the same side as the tumor. The stimulated group showed significantly greater gains in muscle strength right after treatment (average 3.5 vs 2.1) and at 3 months (4.6 vs 3.7). Resting-state MRI showed changes in sensorimotor network organization after stimulation, and changes in an upper limb motor region tracked most closely with recovery.
quick_read: After surgery for a glioma, a common type of brain tumor, some people lose strength on one side of the body. In this study from a large hospital in Beijing, 30 such patients received either real or fake magnetic stimulation aimed at the part of the brain that controls the hand. Those who got the real treatment regained strength faster, and the difference was still there three months later. Brain scans suggested the stimulation helped the movement network reorganize, but the study was small and larger trials are needed.
why_it_matters: It is a randomized, sham-controlled trial showing faster strength recovery with stimulation over the hand area on the operated side, a different approach from the low-frequency stimulation of the healthy side used in earlier studies. With 30 patients at one center, the results need confirmation.
relevance_reason: Randomized human trial targeting hand and arm recovery after glioma surgery.
evidence_level: Human trial (randomized, sham-controlled, 30 patients)
date_note: Published online 2026-03-04 (NeuroImage: Clinical volume 50, 2026).

title: Most severe weakness after surgery near the brain's supplementary motor area improved within 3 months, 15-year study finds
source: Clinical Neurology and Neurosurgery (Haukeland University Hospital, Bergen)
summary: This retrospective single-center cohort followed 46 adults who had grade 2 to 4 gliomas removed in or next to the supplementary motor area (SMA) between 2009 and 2024. On the first day after surgery, 54.3% had severe motor deficits and 56.5% had severe language problems, typical of SMA syndrome; by first follow-up both had fallen to 8.9%. Most patients recovered markedly within 3 months, though some kept mild motor or language difficulties and lower ECOG performance status, and older age was linked to lasting arm weakness. Gross total resection was achieved in 71.7%, 30-day mortality was 0%, 39% went to specialized rehabilitation at discharge, and 85% of those sent home received community rehabilitation.
quick_read: Surgery for tumors near a brain area called the supplementary motor area can cause sudden, dramatic weakness and speech problems right after the operation. This Norwegian study looked back at 46 adults treated over 15 years and found that more than half had severe weakness the day after surgery. By their first follow-up visit, fewer than 1 in 10 still had severe weakness, and most had improved a great deal within three months. Some people kept mild problems, especially older patients with arm weakness, so rehabilitation and planning ahead still matter.
why_it_matters: It gives patients and families a realistic, mostly hopeful picture of recovery after this kind of surgery, and shows how often rehabilitation was needed. It is a small retrospective study from one center, so individual outcomes vary.
relevance_reason: Direct data on recovery of movement after brain tumor surgery, with rehab needs.
evidence_level: Human study (retrospective single-center cohort, 46 patients)
date_note: Published online 2026-07-31; print issue November 2026.

title: Electrical stimulation added to rehab was linked to better facial nerve recovery after surgery for tumors at the base of the brain
summary: This single-center retrospective cohort included adults who had cerebellopontine angle (CPA) tumors removed between 2018 and 2023 with a confirmed facial nerve injury that needed surgical reconstruction. Patients were grouped by the rehabilitation they received in routine care: standard therapy, standard therapy plus transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), or a multimodal plan combining TENS with targeted drug support. Over 12 months, facial function was measured with the House-Brackmann, Yanagihara and Sunnybrook scales, the Facial Disability Index, and surface and needle EMG. All groups improved, the groups with TENS improved more, and the multimodal group showed the largest gains in facial symmetry, voluntary movement and patient-reported function, even after adjusting for other factors.
quick_read: Tumors at the base of the brain, in an area called the cerebellopontine angle, can injure the nerve that moves the face during surgery. This study looked back at patients whose facial nerve had to be repaired during that surgery and compared the rehab they received afterward. Everyone improved over a year, but people whose rehab included mild electrical stimulation through the skin recovered more, and those who also got targeted medication did best. Because patients were not randomly assigned, it shows a link rather than proof, and the authors call for prospective trials.
why_it_matters: Facial weakness is one of the most visible cranial nerve problems after brain tumor surgery, and this points to practical rehab options that may help. The study is retrospective, the number of patients per group is limited, and treatment was not randomized.
relevance_reason: Cranial nerve (facial) deficit after brain tumor surgery with a rehab and stimulation comparison.
evidence_level: Human study (retrospective single-center cohort)
date_note: Published online 2026-03-02; issue dated 2026-07-03. CPA tumors such as vestibular schwannomas sit beside the brainstem at the base of the brain.

title: Supervised strength and endurance training during chemo was safe and improved fitness and quality of life in high-grade glioma
summary: In this prospective, single-arm proof-of-concept trial at several German centers, 54 patients with high-grade glioma took part in Active in Neuro-Oncology (ActiNO), a 16-week program of supervised strength and endurance exercise twice a week during chemotherapy. Physical working capacity rose 23%, peak oxygen uptake 13% and peak power 19%, and quality of life, including global health and physical functioning, improved to normative levels. Exercise-related side effects were few and mild (CTCAE grade 1-2) and adherence was 85%, but 48% dropped out, mainly because of disease progression or physical limits.
quick_read: People with aggressive brain tumors often lose strength and stamina during treatment. In this German study, 54 patients with high-grade glioma did supervised strength and endurance workouts twice a week for 16 weeks while on chemotherapy. Their fitness improved clearly and their quality of life, including physical functioning, rose to levels seen in the general population. Side effects from the exercise were few and mild, though about half of participants did not finish, mostly because of their illness.
why_it_matters: It shows that structured, fairly intense exercise is possible and safe for many people with high-grade glioma during treatment, which supports building it into survivorship and rehab care. There was no control group and many people dropped out, so the size of the benefit is uncertain.
relevance_reason: Neuro-oncology survivorship rehab with physical function and quality of life outcomes.
evidence_level: Human study (prospective single-arm proof-of-concept trial, 54 patients)
date_note: Issue date 2025-11-01 (Neuro-Oncology volume 27, issue 11).

title: NervGen doses first participant in RESTORE, a Phase 3 trial of NVG-291 for hand function in chronic cervical spinal cord injury
summary: NervGen announced that the first participant has been dosed in RESTORE, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 study of NVG-291, an investigational peptide designed to target the inhibitory CSPG-PTP-sigma pathway that can block nerve repair. Participants receive a once-daily injection under the skin (NVG-291 or placebo) for 12 weeks, followed by a 4-week observation period, with an optional open-label extension planned. The primary endpoint is change in hand function measured by the GRASSP Quantitative Prehension score. About 150 adults are expected to enroll across the United States and Canada; the company expects enrollment to finish in the second half of 2027 and topline data in the first half of 2028.
quick_read: This is a large, late-stage study of an experimental drug called NVG-291 in adults who injured the spinal cord in their neck one to ten years ago. The drug is designed to block a natural signal that stops damaged nerves from repairing themselves after an injury. Participants get a daily shot under the skin, either the drug or a dummy shot, for 12 weeks, and researchers measure whether their hand function improves. If it works, it could become one of the first medicines aimed at helping people regain hand use years after a spinal cord injury, but results are not expected until 2028 and injuries not caused by trauma are excluded.
why_it_matters: This is a late-stage drug trial with hand function as its main goal, which is directly relevant to hand recovery after cervical cord damage. Eligibility is limited to traumatic injuries, though: the registry listing excludes nontraumatic spinal cord injury, ongoing cord compression and malignancy within the past 5 years, so tumor-related compression would likely not qualify.
relevance_reason: Phase 3, recruiting, hand-function primary endpoint; high topical relevance even though tumor-related injury appears ineligible.
evidence_level: Human trial (Phase 3 RCT, recruiting; builds on Phase 1b/2a CONNECT SCI)

trial_status.status: Recruiting (registry start 2026-09-28; first participant dosed per 2026-10-12 release)
trial_status.location: Up to 60 sites in the US and Canada; as of the registry check on 2026-10-21, sites in Stamford, CT and Lutherville, MD were listed as recruiting, with 21 more US/Canada sites not yet recruiting

title: First-in-human iPSC-derived neural progenitor cell transplant for subacute spinal cord injury: no tumors over 2-4 years
source: Nature Medicine (Keio University; also covered by The Japan Times)
summary: Keio University researchers report long-term results of a first-in-human, open-label study in which neural stem/progenitor cells made from induced pluripotent stem cells were transplanted into four patients with subacute complete cervical spinal cord injury. The main safety goal was met: no tumor formation or graft-related adverse events were seen over 2 to 4 years of follow-up, and graft sites were stable on imaging. As an exploratory measure, the median motor score improved by 13 points by week 52, and two patients improved in ASIA grade (A to C and A to D). The authors note these gains were numerically greater than spontaneous recovery in a registry cohort, but with only four patients and no control group, effectiveness still has to be tested in further trials.
quick_read: Researchers in Japan turned specially reprogrammed stem cells into young nerve cells and transplanted them into four people with recent, complete spinal cord injuries in the neck. The main goal was safety, and over 2 to 4 years no tumors or other problems caused by the transplanted cells were found. Some patients regained movement, and two moved up on the standard scale doctors use to grade spinal cord injuries. With only four people and no comparison group, no one can yet say the cells caused that improvement. It is an early sign that replacing lost spinal cord cells may be possible to do safely in people.
why_it_matters: It is one of the first long-term human safety readouts for replacing lost spinal cord cells with iPSC-derived cells in the cervical (hand-controlling) region of the cord. It shows the approach can be done in people, though whether it works is still unproven.
relevance_reason: High-profile human data on cell replacement in the cervical cord; small, uncontrolled and limited to acute traumatic injury.
evidence_level: Human trial (Phase 1, open-label, n=4)

title: Thiorphan, an existing drug found by computer screening, boosts corticospinal regrowth and forelimb function after cervical spinal cord injury
summary: UC San Diego researchers used computer screens to find existing compounds that push injured motor neurons toward the embryonic, growth-ready gene-activity state linked to successful regeneration. Their lead hit, thiorphan (a neutral endopeptidase inhibitor that has been tested in humans for another use), increased neurite outgrowth 1.8-fold in cultured adult motor cortex neurons. In rats with severe C5 spinal cord contusions, thiorphan infused into the motor cortex starting 2 weeks after injury, combined with a neural stem cell graft, significantly improved forelimb grasping and increased corticospinal axon regeneration into the graft by about 60%. Thiorphan also increased neurite growth in cultured adult monkey and human cortical neurons.
quick_read: Scientists used computers to search existing drugs for ones that could push injured nerve cells back into a young, growth-ready state, and they found one called thiorphan. In rats with neck-level spinal cord injuries, giving thiorphan into the brain together with a stem cell graft helped more nerve fibers regrow and improved the rats' ability to grip with their front paws. The drug also boosted nerve growth in human and monkey nerve cells grown in the lab. This is still animal and lab research, and the drug currently has to be delivered straight into the brain, so it is a long way from being a treatment people can use.
why_it_matters: The study targets the corticospinal tract, the main pathway for skilled hand movement, and measured forelimb grasping after a cervical-level injury, which makes it relevant to hand function. It is still preclinical, and the drug had to be infused directly into the brain because it does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
relevance_reason: Top-journal regeneration result focused on hand-related motor pathways; animal and cell-culture evidence only.
evidence_level: Animal study plus human/primate cell culture

title: Multichannel 'biomimetic' scaffold matched or beat nerve autografts for bridging long nerve gaps in animals
source: Nature Communications (UC San Diego / VA San Diego)
summary: Researchers built a biodegradable polycaprolactone scaffold packed with many tiny parallel channels that mimic the bundles inside a natural nerve, using a new embossing method that leaves over 70% of the cross-section open for regrowing axons. In 1 cm sciatic nerve gaps in rats and 3 cm gaps in rabbits, the scaffold was equivalent to the gold-standard nerve autograft on axon regeneration, motor neuron-to-muscle reconnection and muscle mass, and it beat simple open-tube conduits on all measures. In the 3 cm rabbit gap, muscle electrical responses were about twofold greater than with autografts. The authors say the device is now in a multicenter randomized clinical trial (NCT06529835), and several authors disclose that they are founders and shareholders in Auxilium Therapeutics, which licensed the technology.
quick_read: When a cut nerve in the arm or leg leaves a gap, surgeons often bridge it with a healthy nerve taken from elsewhere in the patient's body, called an autograft. This team built a dissolvable tube packed with many tiny channels, designed to guide regrowing nerve fibers the way the inside of a real nerve does. In rats and rabbits it worked as well as an autograft for nerve regrowth and reconnecting to muscle, and better than a simple hollow tube. The device is now being tested in people, and if it holds up, patients might one day avoid giving up a healthy nerve to repair a gap. Several of the authors have a financial stake in the company that licensed it.
why_it_matters: An off-the-shelf conduit as good as an autograft could mean no need to harvest a healthy nerve when repairing gaps in the arm and hand. It applies to peripheral nerve gaps rather than to the spinal cord itself.
relevance_reason: Strong preclinical nerve-graft-alternative result now in human testing; peripheral rather than cord or root repair.
evidence_level: Animal study (rat and rabbit); device now in clinical trial

title: Systematic review of 959 patients: how much strength nerve and tendon transfers restore to the arm and hand after cervical spinal cord injury
source: Journal of Hand Surgery Global Online (Northwestern / CU Anschutz / Cleveland Clinic)
summary: This PROSPERO-registered systematic review pooled 51 studies covering 959 patients who had tendon and/or nerve transfer surgery to restore elbow extension, grip, pinch or release after a spinal cord injury. For elbow extension, strength of M3 or better (able to move against gravity) was reported in 68% after nerve transfers, 79% after biceps-to-triceps tendon transfer and 70% after deltoid-to-triceps transfer. For finger flexion, the pooled rate of M3 or better after brachialis-to-anterior interosseous nerve transfer was 50% (95% CI 31-70%), with better results in younger patients, while 78% reached M3 or better after supinator-to-posterior interosseous nerve transfer for finger extension. The authors conclude there is no gold standard, that procedure choice is patient-specific, and that more consistent follow-up measures are needed.
quick_read: This study pooled results from 51 earlier studies covering 959 people who had surgery after a neck-level spinal cord injury to reroute working nerves or tendons to muscles that had stopped working. These operations aim to bring back abilities like straightening the elbow, gripping, pinching and letting go. Depending on the procedure, roughly half to about four in five patients regained enough strength to move the joint against gravity. The authors found no single best surgery, so the right choice depends on the person, but the review gives a realistic picture of what these operations can achieve for arm and hand function.
why_it_matters: It gives an evidence-based overview of how much hand and arm strength surgical rerouting of working nerves and tendons has restored, which is useful background for anyone learning about hand-function reconstruction options.
relevance_reason: Large evidence synthesis focused squarely on hand and arm function after cervical cord injury.
evidence_level: Systematic review (Level III therapeutic evidence)

title: Stanford study recruiting: nerve transfer surgery plus electrical stimulation to improve hand function after cervical spinal cord injury
summary: This Stanford observational study is testing whether brief electrical stimulation of donor nerves during nerve transfer surgery, plus a temporary implanted peripheral nerve stimulator used for 60 days afterward, improves hand motor function and pain compared with past patients who had the same surgery without stimulation. About 10 patients with C6 or C7 injuries rated ASIA A or B will have transfers aimed at restoring finger extension (posterior interosseous nerve) and finger flexion (anterior interosseous nerve). The main outcomes are finger and thumb muscle strength at 36 months and pain at 6 months, and patients are followed for up to 3 years. The registry notes that all care in the study is standard of care rather than experimental.
quick_read: This Stanford study is enrolling about 10 adults with certain neck-level spinal cord injuries who are already having nerve transfer surgery to help their fingers open and close. During the operation, doctors briefly stimulate the donor nerves with electricity, and a small temporary stimulator is then used for 60 days afterward. Researchers will compare finger and thumb strength and pain with past patients who had the same surgery without stimulation. If it helps, adding electrical stimulation could be a simple way to get more out of nerve transfer surgery, though only a narrow group of patients can join.
why_it_matters: It combines two approaches aimed at hand recovery (nerve transfers and electrical stimulation) and is recruiting now. The criteria are narrow, however (ASIA A/B, C6-C7 level, and active malignancy excluded), so individual eligibility would have to be checked with the study team.
relevance_reason: Recruiting study directly targeting finger flexion and extension; single site with narrow criteria.
evidence_level: Human study (prospective observational cohort vs. retrospective controls)

trial_status.location: Stanford University / Stanford Health Care, Palo Alto, CA, USA
trial_status.key_eligibility: Ages 18-65; cervical SCI ASIA A or B at level C6 or C7; planned AIN and PIN nerve transfers; stable function for at least 3 months; excludes active malignancy and implanted electronic devices (see registry).

title: FASTR-TEN randomized trial tests 10 minutes of electrical stimulation during finger nerve repair; Harborview joins as fifth site
source: Checkpoint Surgical press release; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06867185
summary: FASTR-TEN is a multicenter, double-blind, randomized controlled trial testing whether a brief dose of electrical stimulation delivered to a repaired nerve during surgery speeds healing after finger (digital) nerve injuries. It uses Checkpoint Surgical's investigational Regen10 Nerve Regeneration System under an FDA Investigational Device Exemption; the company's related BEST platform received FDA Breakthrough Device designation. Patients get standard surgical repair with or without 10 minutes of stimulation, and outcomes include two-point discrimination, other sensory tests, pain and hand-function questionnaires through 9 months. In February 2026, UW Medicine's Harborview Medical Center enrolled its first patient, bringing the study to five US institutions.
quick_read: This trial is testing whether 10 minutes of electrical stimulation, given to a finger nerve during surgery to repair it, helps the nerve heal faster. People with a recently cut finger nerve get the standard repair, and some are randomly chosen to also get the stimulation, with neither the patients nor the researchers measuring results told who received it. The team then tracks feeling, pain and hand function for 9 months. If it works, brief stimulation could become an easy add-on to nerve repair surgery, though this study only covers fresh finger nerve cuts, not spinal cord damage.
why_it_matters: Brief electrical stimulation is one of the closest-to-clinic ways to speed up nerve regrowth, and this trial tests it rigorously in the hand. It covers fresh finger-nerve cuts repaired within a month of injury, not spinal cord or root compression.
relevance_reason: Rigorous recruiting RCT of a regeneration-boosting technique in the hand; narrow injury type.
evidence_level: Human trial (randomized, double-blind device trial, recruiting)

trial_status.location: Indianapolis IN; Columbia MO; St Louis MO; Columbus OH; Seattle WA (USA)
trial_status.key_eligibility: Ages 18-80; complete digital nerve transection needing repair within 1 month of injury; gap of 10 mm or less; no history of neuropathy (see registry).

title: PEG 'axonal fusion' used with nerve autografts linked to better early sensory recovery in first human comparison
summary: Polyethylene glycol (PEG) is a chemical that, during nerve repair surgery, can help re-seal cut nerve fibers and limit the breakdown of the disconnected segment. This analysis of prospectively collected data compared 48 PEG-assisted upper-extremity nerve repairs, 42 direct (primary) repairs and 6 repairs using a nerve autograft, followed for up to 100 days. Patients in the PEG-plus-autograft group were more likely to reach a meaningful sensory recovery grade (MRCC 3 or higher) over follow-up than those with PEG primary repair (p=0.029). The authors call this the first human comparison of PEG-assisted techniques and say the small autograft group means larger validation studies are needed.
quick_read: When a nerve is cut, the part that is cut off usually breaks down, and the nerve then has to slowly regrow over months. Polyethylene glycol, or PEG, is a chemical used during repair surgery to help seal cut nerve fibers back together right away. This study compared different PEG-assisted repairs of arm and hand nerves and found that patients who had PEG combined with a nerve graft were more likely to regain useful feeling within the first 100 days than those who had PEG with a direct repair. Only 6 patients were in the graft group, so the results are early and need to be confirmed in larger studies.
why_it_matters: PEG fusion aims to reconnect cut nerve fibers right away rather than waiting months for regrowth, and this adds early human data on arm and hand nerves. Only 6 patients received autografts, so the findings are preliminary.
relevance_reason: Human data on a novel nerve-repair technique in the upper limb; small, early, and not about spinal compression.
evidence_level: Human study (prospective cohort subset from a randomized trial; n=48)

title: Tongue-controlled glove that combines a soft robot and electrical muscle stimulation helped five people with cervical spinal cord injury grasp everyday objects
quick_read: People with injuries high in the neck often lose the ability to open and close their hands, and many cannot press buttons or use joysticks to control helper devices. Researchers in Denmark and the Netherlands built a system where the user moves the tongue against a custom mouthpiece to tell a soft robotic glove to close the fingers, and to trigger mild electrical stimulation of the forearm muscles to open the hand. Five people with cervical spinal cord injury tried it on everyday tasks such as picking up a bottle or a toothbrush. With the stimulation version of the glove, 96% of grasp attempts succeeded, and users reported low discomfort, pain and fatigue. It is a small early study, but it shows a practical way to give back daily hand use when the hand itself cannot move well.
summary: The team paired a non-invasive tongue-control interface, built into a fitted dental retainer, with a five-finger soft exoskeleton glove adapted from the commercial Carbonhand glove. Tongue commands drive tendon-based flexion of each finger, and a tongue command also triggers functional electrical stimulation (FES) to extend the fingers and open the hand. Five participants with cervical spinal cord injury tested grasping tasks over two sessions. The overall success rate was 96% with the FES opening exoskeleton and 89% with a passive opening version, and participants reported consistently low discomfort, pain and fatigue and preferred the system for its wearability and ease of use.
why_it_matters: Hand function is a top priority for people with cervical injuries, and this approach works even for people with severe paralysis and long-standing injuries. It is an assistive device that restores use while worn, not a treatment that repairs nerves, and it was tested in only five people.
relevance_reason: Directly targets hand grasp and release after cervical cord injury; very small study and assistive rather than regenerative.
evidence_level: Human study (feasibility evaluation; n=5)

title: Phase 2 results posted for NTX-001, a PEG 'nerve fusion' kit used during repair of freshly cut arm and leg nerves
date_note: Date the trial results were first posted on ClinicalTrials.gov; the study itself was completed in June 2024.
quick_read: When a nerve in the arm or leg is cut, surgeons sew the ends together, but the nerve then has to regrow slowly over months and recovery is often incomplete. NTX-001 is a single-use surgical kit that uses a chemical called polyethylene glycol (PEG) to try to fuse the cut nerve fibers back together right at the time of surgery. In this Phase 2 trial of 51 people with a freshly cut nerve below the shoulder nerve network, patients got either the standard stitched repair or the repair plus NTX-001. At 12 weeks, hand function questionnaire scores improved by about 18 points with NTX-001 versus about 13 points with standard repair, but the registry does not report a statistical test for that difference, so the result should be read as encouraging but unproven. The trial is finished and is not recruiting.
summary: Neuraptive Therapeutics posted results on October 15, 2026 for its randomized, patient- and evaluator-blinded Phase 2a trial (NCT04572906) comparing NTX-001 plus standard suture repair with standard repair alone in acute single transected peripheral nerve injuries below the brachial plexus, repaired within 48 hours. The trial enrolled 51 participants at 10 US sites. For the primary outcome, change in Michigan Hand Questionnaire total score (0 to 100) from baseline to week 12, the mean change was 18.42 (standard error 3.64, n=17) with NTX-001 and 12.80 (standard error 3.04, n=24) with standard care; no p-value is listed for this comparison. Serious adverse events were reported in 2 of 23 NTX-001 participants and 4 of 28 standard-care participants.
why_it_matters: PEG fusion aims to reconnect cut nerve fibers immediately instead of waiting months for regrowth, and this is randomized human data on a packaged product. The difference is modest, the groups are small, and the trial only covered fresh cuts repaired within 48 hours, not older injuries or compression.
relevance_reason: Randomized human trial of a nerve-repair technology for arm and hand nerves; acute cuts only and results are preliminary.
evidence_level: Randomized controlled Phase 2a trial (n=51; results posted on registry, not yet peer reviewed)

trial_status.key_eligibility: Ages 12 to 80 with a single fully transected peripheral nerve below the brachial plexus that can be repaired end to end within 48 hours of injury. Nerve gaps needing a graft were excluded. Tumor-related compression was not part of this trial, which only covered acute cuts.

title: Hand use improved during continued rehabilitation after glioma surgery: one patient's recovery
quick_read: After glioma surgery, one man's hand function worsened while brain swelling increased. His rehabilitation included repeated use of the affected hand, everyday tasks, stretching and occupational therapy. As swelling subsided, grip and dexterity improved; by day 134 he could hang laundry using that hand. This is one case, so it cannot establish which part of treatment caused recovery.
summary: Clinicians followed a 43-year-old man after surgery for recurrent glioma. They tracked brain imaging, grip strength and a block-moving dexterity test. Supervised rehabilitation began in hospital and continued with home practice. Motor performance and imaging measures deteriorated early, then improved as edema decreased. There was no comparison group.
why_it_matters: Useful background for discussions about hand control, task-focused occupational therapy and potentially reversible postoperative swelling. It does not promise recovery or provide a home exercise prescription.
evidence_level: Single adult case report; no control group
date_note: Older research added for its direct relevance to hand function, not a new breakthrough.

title: Writing and daily hand use improved after targeted practice following cerebellar tumor surgery: a case report
quick_read: A woman had difficulty writing and typing after a cerebellar tumor was removed, despite relatively preserved muscle strength. A supervised program practiced useful movements with the affected hand. Writing, task speed and reported daily use improved. This report concerns coordination problems and illustrates that useful hand function involves more than strength alone.
summary: The 42-year-old participant received constraint-induced movement therapy for three hours daily over ten treatment days. Tasks included writing, handling small objects and everyday activities. Standard arm-function measures and her signature improved after treatment. This uncontrolled, single-patient study cannot establish effectiveness for other patients.
why_it_matters: Especially relevant to hand clumsiness, accuracy and coordination after tumor surgery. A rehabilitation specialist must assess suitability; restricting the stronger hand is not an unsupervised exercise recommendation.
evidence_level: Single adult case report; no control group
date_note: Published in 2019; added as directly relevant background, not recent news.

title: Magnetic stimulation trial found an early hand-strength benefit, but no clear overall advantage at three months
quick_read: Thirty people with new arm weakness after brain tumor surgery entered a trial of magnetic brain stimulation or sham stimulation, followed by physical therapy. Hand strength was better in the stimulation group at one month. The main measure of arm recovery at three months did not differ significantly. This suggests a possible early benefit, not a proven lasting recovery treatment.
summary: Participants received seven days of low-frequency stimulation over the unaffected motor cortex or sham treatment. The trial missed its primary three-month Fugl-Meyer outcome. Other functional benefits were limited. This trial also contributes patients to the multicenter analysis already covered on this site, so those reports are not independent evidence.
why_it_matters: Helps readers weigh encouraging hand results against a negative primary outcome when discussing experimental stimulation with clinicians.
evidence_level: Randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial; 30 participants
date_note: Foundational 2024 trial. Its participants overlap with the 2025 multicenter report.

title: Nine children completed intensive affected-arm training after brain tumors, with gains maintained at three months
source: Pediatric Physical Therapy (St. Jude Children's Research Hospital)
quick_read: A small study tested a three-week constraint-induced movement therapy program in children with one-sided arm impairment related to brain tumors. All nine children completed it. The amount and quality of affected-arm use improved, with gains still present at the three-month check. The program was demanding for some families.
summary: Researchers measured arm use, quality of life and parent-reported feasibility before treatment, afterward and at follow-up. There was no randomized comparison group. The results support feasibility in selected children, not proof of effectiveness in adults or everyone with tumor-related hand problems.
why_it_matters: Adds tumor-specific evidence about intensive practice of the affected arm and hand. Age and study size limit how broadly the findings apply.
evidence_level: Pediatric before-and-after pilot; 9 participants; no control group
date_note: The journal gives January 2017 without a specific day; January 1 is used for sorting. Older background research.

title: Physical and occupational therapy during glioma treatment: some benefits, but the main quality-of-life result was inconclusive
source: Physical Therapy / University of Southern Denmark
quick_read: A Danish trial compared supervised physical and occupational therapy with usual rehabilitation during glioma treatment. It enrolled 64 people who were functionally independent. After six weeks, the main overall quality-of-life measure was not significantly better with the program. Some secondary measures, including fatigue, thinking-related functioning and aerobic capacity, favored rehabilitation.
summary: Thirty-two participants were assigned to each group. Recruitment and follow-up were insufficient to determine superiority for the primary outcome. The study supports further evaluation of rehabilitation during cancer treatment but does not establish a specific treatment for loss of hand control.
why_it_matters: Rehabilitation can be considered during ongoing treatment, with goals matched to the person's abilities. Promising secondary results should not be confused with a positive primary endpoint.
evidence_level: Single-blind randomized controlled trial; 64 participants
date_note: Older controlled research added as background.

title: Motor skills and daily activities improved during intensive rehabilitation after brain tumor surgery
quick_read: A hospital reviewed 35 adults receiving intensive rehabilitation after brain tumor surgery. Movement, thinking and everyday-function measures improved during their stay, with gains similar to those seen in a stroke rehabilitation comparison group. Both benign and malignant tumor groups improved. Because everyone received rehabilitation, the study cannot separate treatment effects from natural recovery.
summary: Therapy included physical and occupational rehabilitation, with upper-limb and everyday-task training. The retrospective analysis compared tumor patients with 108 stroke patients receiving similar care. Family caregivers generally reported satisfaction later. There was no untreated brain-tumor comparison group.
why_it_matters: Supports considering a rehabilitation assessment after tumor surgery, including goals for useful arm function and independence. It does not predict an individual's outcome.
evidence_level: Retrospective cohort; 35 brain-tumor patients and 108 stroke comparators
date_note: Published online April 30, 2019; added as background research.

title: Hand dexterity after brain tumor surgery was linked to changes in brain-network connections
quick_read: A small study followed hand coordination and brain scans before and after surgery in 16 people with brain lesions. Better and worse dexterity recovery were associated with different patterns of communication between brain networks. This concerns skilled hand use, not just shaking or muscle strength. It suggests research targets, rather than a proven new treatment.
summary: Researchers used the nine-hole peg test and resting-state MRI. Changes in connections within and between movement and attention networks differed between recovery groups.
why_it_matters: Useful for understanding why fine hand control can remain difficult even when strength is relatively preserved.
evidence_level: Observational cohort, 16 participants
limitation: Association cannot establish cause or show that changing these connections improves recovery.
care_question: Could we measure my dexterity separately from strength and set specific occupational-therapy goals?

title: Early magnetic stimulation was associated with faster recovery after surgery in the supplementary motor area
quick_read: Researchers reviewed recovery in 14 people after tumor surgery in a brain region involved in movement. Starting navigated magnetic stimulation within five days was associated with faster recovery from temporary weakness. This was a small retrospective study. It cannot establish that stimulation caused the improvement.
summary: The authors compared postoperative recovery trajectories and reported an association between earlier stimulation and accelerated motor recovery.
why_it_matters: Adds tumor-specific evidence, while leaving the best timing and effectiveness unresolved.
evidence_level: Retrospective observational cohort, 14 participants
limitation: Temporary postoperative weakness may improve naturally; a controlled prospective trial is needed.
care_question: Is my movement difficulty related to the supplementary motor area, and is specialist rehabilitation or a trial appropriate?

title: Small brain tumor study examines the safety of high-frequency magnetic stimulation after surgery
quick_read: Ten people received magnetic stimulation after surgery near movement-related brain areas. Four received high-frequency stimulation on the operated side and six received a different protocol. No seizures or heating effects were reported. The small sample cannot rule out uncommon risks or prove treatment effectiveness.
summary: Strength and daily-function scores improved in both groups. Reported events included a wound revision, a brief fainting episode and temporary altered sensation.
why_it_matters: Safety questions matter before a promising rehabilitation technique can be tested more widely.
evidence_level: Small nonrandomized clinical series, 10 participants
limitation: This is preliminary safety evidence, not proof that the treatment is safe or effective for everyone.
care_question: Would my seizure history, surgical wound or implanted devices affect eligibility for stimulation research?

title: Review of 31 studies finds exercise feasible after brain tumors, with effectiveness still uncertain
quick_read: A review gathered 31 studies of exercise in people with brain tumors. Participants could take part in strength, aerobic, balance and other programs, with possible benefits for function and quality of life. Most studies were small or at high risk of bias. The review supports more research and individually planned rehabilitation, not a single exercise prescription.
summary: Studies were identified through December 2025. Their varied methods and outcomes prevented a simple pooled answer about clinical effectiveness.
why_it_matters: Provides a broader view than one positive exercise study.
evidence_level: Systematic review, 31 heterogeneous studies
limitation: Feasibility does not establish the best program or guarantee improvement.
care_question: Can a rehabilitation professional adapt exercise around my weakness, fatigue and treatment schedule?

title: Brain tumor rehabilitation review calls for earlier referrals and continuing support
quick_read: Researchers reviewed 17 documents about rehabilitation after a primary brain tumor. Recommendations generally supported multidisciplinary care for movement, thinking and communication difficulties. They also identified inconsistent referrals and a shortage of tumor-specific pathways. This is a review of guidance, not a test of a new treatment.
summary: The review included five guideline or consensus documents and twelve contextual sources, searched through December 2025.
why_it_matters: Helps readers ask about rehabilitation as part of ongoing care rather than only immediately after surgery.
evidence_level: Scoping review of guidelines and supporting evidence
limitation: Recommendations are broader than the limited evidence for individual rehabilitation techniques.
care_question: Could I have a rehabilitation assessment and a plan for reassessment as my needs change?

title: Blood-cell mitochondria improved nerve repair in rat experiments
quick_read: Researchers isolated mitochondria, the energy-producing parts of cells, from blood immune cells. They tested them in rats with crushed nerves or surgically bridged nerve gaps. Several measures of nerve and muscle recovery improved. This is laboratory and animal research, with no demonstrated treatment benefit in patients.
summary: Rat experiments assessed nerve structure, electrical responses and walking. Human-derived mitochondria were also studied experimentally, not as a clinical treatment.
why_it_matters: Blood could be a less invasive source than harvesting muscle or other tissue if the approach eventually proves useful.
evidence_level: Preclinical cell experiments and rat injury models
limitation: Human safety, dosing and clinical effectiveness remain unknown.
care_question: Is there any registered human trial for this approach, or is it still preclinical?

title: After hand nerve repair, brain maps changed without a clear link to functional impairment
quick_read: MRI mapped finger responses in 21 people with repaired hand nerves and 30 controls. Brain representations of the fingers were less orderly after repair. Importantly, the researchers found no credible link between these map changes and functional impairment. A different-looking scan does not by itself explain how well a hand works.
summary: Changes appeared in the brain representation of the repaired hand and, unexpectedly, the uninjured hand.
why_it_matters: Shows why direct measures of sensation and hand use matter alongside imaging.
evidence_level: Human observational imaging study, 21 patients and 30 controls
limitation: The study did not test a rehabilitation treatment.
care_question: Which practical tests can track sensation and hand function during my recovery?

title: Experimental neural bypass enabled hand movement and sensation in one person with tetraplegia
quick_read: An experimental system combined implanted brain electrodes, muscle stimulation and brain-and-spinal neuromodulation. One person with complete tetraplegia could perform assisted tasks including self-feeding and delicate object handling. Some elbow-strength and wrist-sensation improvements persisted without stimulation. This is an early demonstration in spinal cord injury, not evidence for brain tumor recovery.
summary: The hybrid system linked movement intention to assistance and provided sensory feedback.
why_it_matters: Explores both immediate assistance and lasting recovery rather than treating them as the same result.
evidence_level: First-in-human experimental study, one participant
limitation: One participant cannot establish general effectiveness; the system requires invasive and specialized technology.
care_question: Does this research address my diagnosis, and what registered trials have eligibility criteria relevant to me?

title: Soft wearable robot helped arm movement during use after brachial plexus injury
quick_read: A soft shoulder-and-elbow exosuit was tested in 14 adults with longstanding traumatic brachial plexus injury. Movement range and endurance improved while assistance was active. A subgroup of four also improved on functional tasks. The study assessed immediate help, not lasting recovery after the device was removed.
summary: Six participants had complete lesions and ten had previously undergone nerve transfer surgery.
why_it_matters: Assistive technology may help everyday movement even when it has not been shown to regenerate nerves.
evidence_level: Single-session human feasibility study, 14 participants
limitation: Long-term rehabilitation effects and independent everyday use were not evaluated.
care_question: Would an assistive device help my daily tasks, and how would we distinguish assistance from recovery?

title: Gene-regulation target improved optic-nerve cell survival in preclinical research
quick_read: Researchers investigated a gene-regulating protein called Pou2f2 in retinal nerve cells. Increasing its activity improved cell survival and nerve-fiber growth after experimental optic-nerve injury. Retinal function was partly preserved in the model. This is preclinical work, not a therapy shown to restore human vision.
summary: The work combined retinal-cell experiments, gene-expression analyses and experimental optic-nerve injury.
why_it_matters: Identifies a possible target for future nerve-protection and regeneration research.
evidence_level: Preclinical retinal-cell and animal injury research
limitation: No human treatment benefit has been established.
care_question: Has this approach reached a registered human study for my specific eye condition?

title: Daily independence improved during rehabilitation after meningioma treatment, adult study finds
quick_read: Researchers reviewed 151 adults receiving rehabilitation after treatment for a meningioma, a type of brain tumor; most had surgery. Functional outcomes were analyzed in 53 with measurable daily-living limitations on admission. Their independence scores improved during rehabilitation. Without an untreated comparison group, the study cannot separate rehabilitation effects from natural recovery.
summary: In the 53-person subgroup, average Barthel Index scores rose from 66.8 to 75.2. Improvements in dressing, mobility and stair climbing remained significant after adjustment for multiple comparisons.
why_it_matters: Adds tumor-specific evidence about daily independence after treatment.
evidence_level: Adult single-center retrospective cohort; 151 reviewed, 53 in functional-outcome analysis
limitation: No untreated comparison group. This does not establish a specific treatment for hand clenching or demonstrate nerve regeneration.
care_question: Could multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation address my daily-function goals, and how would improvement be measured?
date_note: Background research published February 26, 2026, added October 23, 2026. This is not a new study announcement today.
relevance_reason: Tumor-specific rehabilitation and daily-function outcomes; observational evidence, not a hand-specific intervention.

title: UK nationwide study of trametinib and dabrafenib in children with low-grade glioma reports tumor control and vision outcomes
quick_read: Doctors at 7 UK children's brain tumor centers reviewed 50 young patients with low-grade glioma who took the targeted pills trametinib and dabrafenib between 2016 and 2024, outside of clinical trials. About 3.5 years after starting, 96% were alive and 38% had seen their tumor grow again. On MRI, 74% had a benefit: 20% of tumors shrank and 54% stayed stable. Among 35 children whose tumor involved the optic (vision) pathway, 72% had their vision stabilize or improve. This is a look back at routine care, not a randomized trial.
summary: This retrospective national review covered patients under 18 treated with MAPK inhibitor therapy at 7 UK pediatric brain tumor centers from 2016 to 2024. It assessed MRI response, visual response in optic pathway tumours, overall and progression-free survival, side effects, dose reductions and early stopping. At a median of 3.5 years from starting treatment, overall survival was 96% and 38% had progressed. Radiological benefit was 74% (partial response 20%, stable disease 54%). Of 35 patients with optic pathway tumours, 72% had visual benefit (63% stable, 9% improved). The authors also compared how long the response lasted on MAPK inhibitors versus prior chemotherapy and concluded the drugs were safe and effective, with longer periods without progression than earlier chemotherapy.
why_it_matters: Low-grade gliomas near the visual pathways can damage vision and other nerve functions, so real-world data on tumor control and vision with targeted pills helps families ask informed questions about treatment options.
evidence_level: Retrospective multicenter real-world cohort (n=50); no control group
limitation: Not randomized, and most children had already had other treatments. Holding vision steady was more common than improving it, and the study does not show nerve regeneration.
care_question: Would a MAPK inhibitor be suitable for this tumor's genetic type, and how would vision and nerve function be monitored during treatment?
date_note: Research published April 8, 2026, added October 24, 2026. This is not a new study announcement today.
relevance_reason: Tumor-specific targeted therapy with vision (optic nerve pathway) outcomes; observational.

title: Recruiting in Seoul: home smart-glove hand rehabilitation trial that includes people with weakness after a brain tumor
date_note: Date the trial was first posted on ClinicalTrials.gov; the record was last updated April 24, 2026 and still shows Recruiting.
quick_read: Samsung Medical Center in Seoul is testing whether a game-based smart glove used at home helps arm and hand movement more than a standard home exercise workbook. Adults with one-sided weakness for more than 3 months after a stroke, brain injury or brain tumor can qualify. Each group trains 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week, for 4 weeks. The main result will be the change in an arm and hand movement score. The trial is recruiting and plans to enroll 40 people.
summary: NCT06837324 is a randomized, parallel-group trial with a blinded outcomes assessor comparing home-based training with the Neofect Smart Glove against home occupational therapy using a research-team workbook. Both groups complete 20 sessions of 30 minutes (once daily, 5 days a week, 4 weeks). The primary outcome is improvement in the upper-limb Fugl-Meyer score. The study started April 11, 2025, with estimated completion December 31, 2026, and a target enrollment of 40.
why_it_matters: Most hand rehabilitation trials only accept stroke patients. This one explicitly includes weakness caused by a brain tumor and is done at home.
evidence_level: Randomized controlled trial in progress (no results yet)
limitation: Single site in South Korea, small, short 4-week program. No results have been posted.
care_question: Would home-based, device-guided hand training be a reasonable addition to my current therapy, and are similar programs available near me?
relevance_reason: Recruiting hand rehabilitation trial that explicitly accepts brain tumor related weakness; single site abroad.

trial_status.location: Samsung Medical Center, Seoul, South Korea
trial_status.key_eligibility: Ages 19 to 85 with one-sided weakness (hemiparesis) lasting more than 3 months from stroke, traumatic brain injury or brain tumor, so tumor-related weakness qualifies. Wrist and finger stiffness must be mild (Modified Ashworth Scale 1+ or lower) and K-MMSE score at least 21. Excluded: severe stiffness (MAS 3 or more), pain above 6 out of 10, major psychiatric disorders, or vision too poor to see the screen.

title: Recruiting in Seoul: home smart-board shoulder and arm rehabilitation trial that includes people with weakness after a brain tumor
date_note: Date the trial was first posted on ClinicalTrials.gov; the record was last updated April 24, 2026 and still shows Recruiting.
quick_read: A sister trial at Samsung Medical Center is testing a game-based smart board for practicing arm and shoulder movements at home, compared with a standard home exercise workbook. Adults with one-sided weakness for more than 3 months after a stroke, brain injury or brain tumor can qualify if they can lift the shoulder somewhat. Each group trains 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week, for 4 weeks. The trial is recruiting and plans to enroll 40 people.
summary: NCT06837363 is a randomized, parallel-group trial with a blinded outcomes assessor comparing home-based training with the Neofect Smart Board against home occupational therapy using a research-team workbook. Both groups complete 20 sessions of 30 minutes (once daily, 5 days a week, 4 weeks). The primary outcome is improvement in the upper-limb Fugl-Meyer score. The study started April 1, 2025, with estimated completion December 31, 2026, and a target enrollment of 40.
why_it_matters: It is one of few arm rehabilitation trials that names brain tumor as a qualifying cause of weakness.
evidence_level: Randomized controlled trial in progress (no results yet)
limitation: Single site in South Korea, small, short 4-week program. No results have been posted.
care_question: Is my shoulder strength enough for this kind of training, and could a home device program support my therapy goals?
relevance_reason: Recruiting arm rehabilitation trial that explicitly accepts brain tumor related weakness; single site abroad.

trial_status.location: Samsung Medical Center, Seoul, South Korea
trial_status.key_eligibility: Ages 19 to 85 with one-sided weakness lasting more than 3 months from stroke, traumatic brain injury or brain tumor, so tumor-related weakness qualifies. Shoulder flexor and adductor strength must be at least MRC grade 2, shoulder stiffness mild (MAS 1+ or lower), and K-MMSE at least 21. Excluded: severe stiffness (MAS 3 or more), pain above 6 out of 10, major psychiatric disorders, or vision too poor to see the screen.

title: Most long-term survivors of low-grade glioma surgery kept good daily function after 15 or more years, French series reports
quick_read: A surgeon in Montpellier, France reviewed 103 adults who had brain mapping-guided surgery for a slow-growing glioma and were followed for at least 15 years. About 90% returned to work after surgery, and only 3 had a lasting new deficit, a planned loss of part of the visual field. After an average of 18 years, 86 were alive and 90.7% of them still had good everyday function. Patients who had radiotherapy were less likely to keep working and to keep good function. This is one surgeon's experience looked at in hindsight.
summary: The series included 103 patients operated on with intraoperative electrical mapping (selected from a database of operations performed from 1996 onward) who had at least 15 years of follow-up after surgery. Mean postoperative Karnofsky score was 94.8 and 81 patients (90%) returned to work. Sixty-three patients (61.2%) had repeat surgery, with a neurological morbidity rate of 1.5% across 205 operations. Mean follow-up was 18.2 years with overall survival of 83.5%; 78 of 86 survivors (90.7%) had a Karnofsky score of 80 or higher. Early radiotherapy was associated with a lower return-to-work rate, and irradiated patients were less likely to have a Karnofsky score of 80 or higher at last follow-up.
why_it_matters: It gives rare very long-term data on whether people keep their function and independence after brain tumor surgery that tries to protect working brain networks.
evidence_level: Single-surgeon retrospective consecutive series (n=103) from a prospective database
limitation: One surgeon, one center, no comparison group, and no detailed cognitive testing. Most patients had little deficit before surgery, so it does not show recovery of existing nerve damage.
care_question: How do surgery, radiotherapy and their timing affect long-term function for my tumor type?
date_note: Research published online September 12, 2025, added October 24, 2026. This is not a new study announcement today.
relevance_reason: Long-term function and survivorship after brain tumor surgery; not focused on repairing established nerve damage.

title: Review of 121 published cases compares treatments for Holmes tremor, a tremor that can follow brain injuries including tumors
quick_read: Holmes tremor is a slow, coarse shaking that can appear weeks or months after damage deep in the brain, from causes such as stroke, injury or tumors. Researchers pooled 121 published cases to see which treatments helped. Deep brain stimulation helped in all 40 cases where it was used, and dopamine-boosting drugs helped some people. Some cases improved when the underlying cause was treated. Because the evidence comes from case reports, successes are likely over-reported.
summary: The scoping review gathered 121 cases from 97 publications. Levodopa was used in 67 cases, with improvement in 21 (31.34%). Dopamine agonists had positive results in 10 of 11 cases, anticholinergics in 7 of 24, and botulinum toxin in 1 of 5, while beta blockers (17 cases) gave no satisfactory response. Lesion surgery gave satisfactory control in 6 of 8 cases and deep brain stimulation was positive in all 40 cases. Fourteen cases responded to treatment of the underlying disease, including some tumors and hydrocephalus. The authors propose levodopa, trihexyphenidyl and dopamine agonists as first-line options and advise not delaying surgical referral if medication fails.
why_it_matters: Tremor from deep brain damage is hard to treat, and this review lays out which options have been tried and how often they helped.
evidence_level: Scoping review of case reports and case series (121 cases)
limitation: Based mostly on individual case reports, so publication bias is likely and response rates are not reliable estimates. It covers all causes, not tumors alone.
care_question: If tremor develops after a brain lesion, which medicines should be tried first, and when should a referral for deep brain stimulation be considered?
date_note: Review published June 17, 2025, added October 24, 2026. This is not a new study announcement today.
relevance_reason: Covers a movement problem that can follow deep brain lesions including tumors; mixed causes and case-report evidence.

title: Recruiting Baltimore trial tests personalized stimulation with hand, arm or walking therapy for cerebellar damage, including tumors
quick_read: A Baltimore study is testing whether personalized, non-invasive electrical brain stimulation adds benefit to intensive rehabilitation for adults with damage mainly affecting the cerebellum, the brain region important for coordination. The registry explicitly includes damage from tumors, as well as stroke or degeneration, and participants choose a therapy focus such as hand dexterity and arm control, walking and balance, or speech. It plans to compare active stimulation with sham stimulation in 30 adults aged 18–75; both groups receive therapy. No results are posted, and a history of seizures is an exclusion, so this is an experimental research option rather than a proven way to restore hand use.
summary: IMPACT (NCT07642856) at the Motion Analysis Lab in Kennedy Krieger Institute, Baltimore, is a randomized, parallel-group study of personalized transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) paired with individualized rehabilitation for cerebellar damage. The protocol describes neuroimaging and electric-field modeling to choose stimulation sites, then checking tolerance and MRI response before proceeding to training. Active and sham arms each include one hour of therapy twice daily, up to 30 sessions over three weeks, with 20 minutes of active or sham stimulation daily. Participants choose walking/balance, hand dexterity/arm control, or speech as a therapy domain. The two primary outcomes are the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA) and patient-reported PROM-Ataxia, measured before and after treatment and at three and six months. These include hand-coordination or dexterity components but are broader ataxia outcomes, not an isolated grasp/release endpoint. Estimated enrollment is 30, with no results posted. The structured design field specifies participant-only masking, while the narrative calls the trial double-blind; that inconsistency needs clarification from the study team.
why_it_matters: This is a tumor-inclusive rehabilitation study that explicitly addresses hand dexterity and arm control, rather than tremor alone. It is a potential research route only when cerebellar involvement is established; hand clenching, numbness or weakness alone does not establish that diagnosis or eligibility.
relevance_reason: Explicit tumor-related cerebellar eligibility and a hand-dexterity/arm-control therapy track; registered US research contact.
evidence_level: Recruiting randomized, sham-controlled trial; 30 adults planned; no results posted
