title: Holmes tremor linked to hydrocephalus from a midbrain tumor improved with treatment: child's case and review of 9 patients
source: Journal of Neurosurgery: Pediatrics (University of British Columbia)
quick_read: Holmes tremor is a hard-to-treat shaking that happens both at rest and during movement, usually after damage near the midbrain. Doctors in Vancouver described a child whose Holmes tremor came from fluid build-up in the brain (hydrocephalus) caused by a tumor in the tectal area of the midbrain, and whose tremor responded to treatment. They also gathered every similar published case they could find, nine patients in total. Draining the fluid (CSF diversion) and levodopa, a Parkinson's drug, were the treatments used most often and were the most effective in this small group, and eye movement problems (Parinaud's syndrome) were common alongside the tremor.
summary: Video case report plus systematic review (MEDLINE and Web of Science to August 2021) of Holmes tremor presenting with hydrocephalus. The index case was a child with low-pressure obstructive hydrocephalus secondary to a tectal tumor whose tremor was treatment-responsive. Nine patients were identified in total; all had a triventriculomegaly pattern with at least some obstructive hydrocephalus, and 4 had low-pressure hydrocephalus. Parinaud's syndrome and bradykinesia were the most commonly associated signs. Levodopa and CSF diversion were the most commonly used and effective treatments. The authors list CSF diversion, antiparkinsonian drugs, antiepileptic drugs, deep brain stimulation and MR-guided focused ultrasound as options, aimed at the nigrostriatal and dentatorubrothalamic pathways thought to be involved.
why_it_matters: It ties Holmes tremor to hydrocephalus and midbrain tumors specifically, and points to treatments (shunt or drainage review, levodopa) that may be overlooked when tremor is treated like ordinary tremor.
relevance_reason: Tumor-related Holmes tremor with hydrocephalus and midbrain eye signs; practical treatment comparison.
evidence_level: Single case report plus systematic review of 9 published cases; not registered, no funding
date_note: Back-catalog item added 2026-10-25. Published online 2022-02-11 (print issue May 2022). Literature searched to August 2021.
limitation: Only nine patients in total, mostly individual case reports, so the authors say the evidence is weak. Results may not apply to tremor that has lasted many years or to tremor without active hydrocephalus.
care_question: Could shunt function or ventricle size be contributing to the tremor, and has a trial of levodopa been considered for a Holmes-type tremor?

title: St. Jude study of 158 medulloblastoma survivors: posterior fossa syndrome after surgery left lasting movement and daily-living problems
source: JAMA Network Open (St. Jude Children's Research Hospital)
quick_read: Posterior fossa syndrome is a complication of surgery for tumors at the back of the brain that can affect speech, movement, mood and memory. Researchers at St. Jude followed 158 adults and teens treated for the childhood brain tumor medulloblastoma, on average about 14 years later. The 37 who had developed the syndrome scored worse on attention, motor and visual-motor speed, and physical performance, and were 8 times more likely to need help with routine daily needs. Even when the early symptoms seem to clear, this suggests survivors may need long-term checks and tailored therapy.
summary: Retrospective cohort of childhood medulloblastoma survivors diagnosed 1985 to 2012 and more than 5 years from diagnosis, treated at one tertiary center. Of 158 participants (median age at assessment 25), 37 (23%) had posterior fossa syndrome and 121 did not, with no differences in age at diagnosis, radiation dose or age at assessment. Median follow-up was 14.2 years. In adjusted models, the syndrome was associated with worse focused attention, motor-processing speed, cognitive flexibility, visuomotor processing speed and physical performance scores, and higher odds of needing assistance with routine daily needs (odds ratio 8.00).
why_it_matters: It shows that tumor-surgery-related motor and coordination problems can persist for decades, which supports ongoing rehabilitation and surveillance for long-term brain tumor survivors.
relevance_reason: Long-term motor and functional outcomes in childhood brain tumor survivors.
evidence_level: Retrospective cohort study, 158 survivors, single center
date_note: Published 2026-02-02; added 2026-10-25 as a strong recent item not yet on the site.
limitation: Medulloblastoma survivors who also had radiation and chemotherapy; it describes outcomes and does not test any treatment. Results may not apply to other tumor types or locations.
care_question: Should a long-term survivor have a formal physical, motor and daily-living assessment, even years after treatment?

title: Brain scans before glioma surgery predicted who would regain movement, by measuring how the opposite side of the brain compensates
quick_read: When a glioma grows in the brain's movement areas, the brain may try to compensate using other regions. Researchers in Beijing used MRI before surgery in 70 people with gliomas in motor areas to measure how flexibly the movement area on the opposite side of the brain was working, and how intact the nerve fibers connecting the two halves were. People with more flexible opposite-side motor cortex recovered movement better at 3 months, while more damage to a middle part of the connecting fibers (corpus callosum) went with worse movement. A combined score predicted severe weakness well, which could one day help plan surgery and rehabilitation for each person.
summary: Retrospective study of 70 patients with motor area gliomas and 23 healthy controls, all with preoperative 3T resting-state fMRI and diffusion MRI. A structural decoupling index (SDI) measured how far functional activity departs from structural connectivity; corpus callosum integrity and disconnection were assessed with tractography. Motor strength (Medical Research Council scale) was measured before surgery and at 3 months. Higher SDI in the contralateral precentral gyrus was associated with better motor recovery, and greater disconnection of the anterior midbody of the corpus callosum (CC4) with poorer motor function. IDH-wildtype status, higher CC4 disconnection and lower contralateral SDI independently predicted severe motor impairment; a combined nomogram had a C-index of 0.914.
why_it_matters: It gives evidence that the healthy side of the brain helps compensate for tumor-related motor damage, and offers a possible way to tailor rehabilitation before surgery.
relevance_reason: Mechanism of motor compensation and recovery prediction after brain tumor surgery.
evidence_level: Retrospective imaging study, 70 patients; prediction model not yet validated in a separate group
date_note: Published online ahead of print 2026-10-02.
limitation: Supratentorial motor-area gliomas only, short 3-month follow-up, and a retrospective single-group model that needs outside validation. It predicts recovery but does not test a treatment.
care_question: Can imaging of the brain's motor networks help guide what kind of rehabilitation is likely to help?

title: Prospective study: hidden strokes and swelling after glioma surgery, often near the thalamus, were linked to lasting disability
source: Journal of Neuro-Oncology (Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center)
quick_read: Surgery to remove a glioma can sometimes injure nearby brain tissue, which may explain some new weakness or other problems afterward. Doctors in Guangzhou scanned 64 people repeatedly in the four weeks after glioma surgery. About 1 in 5 had a small stroke (infarction) after surgery, all in deep regions such as the basal ganglia, thalamus or insula, and swelling and tiny bleeds were common. At four weeks, 13 of 53 assessed patients had some disability, which was linked to heavier blood loss during surgery and to these post-surgery strokes.
summary: Prospective observational study of patients with newly diagnosed supratentorial gliomas undergoing resection, with MRI within 72 hours and on postoperative days 7, 14 and 28. Of 64 patients, 14 (21.9%) had postoperative infarction, all in the basal ganglia, thalamus or insular regions; intraoperative blood loss of 300 mL or more was independently associated with infarction (OR 4.62). Microhemorrhage occurred in 53.8%. Edema occurred in all cases, either residual tumor-associated (decreasing over time, n = 42) or new surgery-induced (increasing over time, n = 22). Of 53 patients assessed at day 28, 13 had disability (mRS 2 or more), associated with higher blood loss (OR 8.88) and postoperative infarction (OR 6.33).
why_it_matters: It helps explain why some people have new deficits after brain tumor surgery and highlights deep-brain strokes as a preventable cause.
relevance_reason: Causes of new neurological deficits after brain tumor surgery, including thalamic injury.
evidence_level: Prospective observational study, 64 patients, single center
date_note: Published 2026-10-13.
limitation: Small single-center study with only 28 days of follow-up and a general disability scale; it does not study recovery or rehabilitation over time.
care_question: Did post-surgery MRI show any small strokes or swelling that could explain new weakness, and what does that mean for expected recovery?

title: Johns Hopkins review: practical guide to managing side effects and resistance with BRAF-targeted drugs for glioma
source: CNS Oncology (Johns Hopkins and Cooper University Health Care)
quick_read: Some gliomas carry a change in the BRAF gene that can be targeted with pills such as dabrafenib with trametinib, or tovorafenib for some children. This review from Johns Hopkins neurologists explains how doctors choose these drugs based on the exact BRAF change, and how to prevent and manage side effects, including lowering the dose, so people can stay on treatment. It notes that tumors can grow again when the drugs are paused or stopped, but some patients respond when the drug is restarted. Newer BRAF drugs and combinations are being tested for tumors that stop responding.
summary: Narrative review of BRAF inhibitor therapy in BRAF-altered low- and high-grade glioma. Key points: treatment should be tailored to the specific BRAF alteration; dabrafenib plus trametinib is FDA-approved for BRAF V600E-mutant gliomas, and tovorafenib is approved for pediatric LGG with BRAF V600 mutations or fusions. Proactive toxicity management, including anticipatory guidance and dose reduction for some patients, is emphasized to avoid interruptions. Pediatric LGG often responds durably, while adults with LGG and patients with HGG often develop resistance. Progression can occur during interruptions or after stopping, though some patients respond to rechallenge. Emerging strategies include combinations with radiation, autophagy inhibitors and other targeted agents, and next-generation BRAF inhibitors (paradox breakers, dimer disruptors, protein degraders) in clinical testing.
why_it_matters: For people whose brain tumor is controlled with targeted drugs, staying on treatment safely protects the nerve function they still have, and this review lays out how that is managed.
relevance_reason: Practical BRAF/MEK targeted therapy management for BRAF-altered low-grade glioma.
evidence_level: Narrative review for clinicians
date_note: Published online 2026-08-03 (December 2026 issue).
limitation: A review, not new trial data. It focuses on tumor control and drug side effects, not on recovering movement or nerve function.
care_question: If a BRAF-targeted drug was stopped or paused, what is the plan if the tumor changes, and would rechallenge be an option?

title: Small pediatric brain tumor trial found mixed balance results with supervised exercise games
quick_read: Supervised balance games were compared with conventional exercises in childhood brain tumor survivors. Walking and one balance test favored games after eight weeks. Another primary balance measure did not show a statistically clear advantage.
summary: Thirty children were randomized; 23 completed treatment, 13 with games and 10 with conventional exercises. Eligibility was ages 6–15. Both groups received twice-weekly physiotherapist-supervised sessions. Timed Up and Go favored games, but the between-group center-of-gravity change was nonsignificant (p=0.075).
why_it_matters: Supports discussing individualized balance rehabilitation, without assuming that games improve every movement problem.
relevance_reason: Tumor-specific pediatric balance rehabilitation.
evidence_level: Small randomized controlled trial; pediatric evidence
date_note: Background research, published 2024-04-10; added 2026-10-25.
limitation: Unequal dropout, baseline balance imbalance and no long-term follow-up limit confidence. Hand recovery was not tested. The paper gives a placeholder registry ID, so registration and recruitment could not be verified; this is not a recruiting opportunity.
care_question: Could supervised balance training address walking difficulties safely?

title: Psilocybin reshaped mouse brain connections through a pathway distinct from a hallucination-related behavior
quick_read: Researchers watched psilocybin alter connections between brain cells in living mice. It promoted new connections and their maturation while also increasing removal of some older connections. Genetic experiments separated this remodeling from the mouse head-twitch response, a laboratory proxy for psychedelic activity. This is a mechanism study, not evidence that psilocybin restores hand function or treats brain tumors.
summary: Baker, Kogan and colleagues manipulated serotonin 5-HT2A receptors in cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons. Restoring receptors only in these cells restored structural remodeling without restoring head-twitch behavior; deleting them prevented remodeling while preserving that behavior. The findings distinguish cellular pathways in mice. University explanation: https://news.ucsc.edu/2026/10/how-psilocybin-reshapes-brain-circuits/
why_it_matters: Helps researchers investigate whether future compounds could promote plasticity with fewer perceptual effects. New synapses are not proof of useful functional recovery.
evidence_level: Peer-reviewed mouse imaging and genetic experiments; no human recovery trial
date_note: Original paper published 2026-10-15; university report dated 2026-10-22. Earlier preprint DOI 10.64898/2026.04.06.716778 concerns the same work, not independent replication.
limitation: Head twitch cannot establish what mice perceive or prove hallucination-free treatment in humans. No tumor-related motor rehabilitation, grasp/release recovery or human safety benefit was established. Claims here were checked against the published abstract and university report; full journal text was inaccessible.
care_question: What human functional outcomes would need testing before this mechanism could inform neurological rehabilitation?

title: Supervised psilocybin study found movement tasks feasible in healthy adults, with limits at higher exposure
source: CNS Drugs; companion analysis in Psychopharmacology
quick_read: A supervised study in 13 healthy adults tested whether people could complete movement tasks during psilocybin's acute effects. Tasks included hand dexterity, arm performance and mobility. Higher exposure impaired some tasks combining movement and thinking, and one participant could not complete several tasks. The study explored feasibility and safety, not whether the drug repairs an injured hand.
summary: In this phase 1 study, dose order was randomized and participants, physiotherapists and statisticians were blinded. There was no placebo-only comparison. Tasks were generally feasible through 15 mg; impairment appeared at 20 mg. Nausea and headache were common; no serious adverse events or movement-task-related adverse events occurred. A companion subset analysis found small time-dependent dexterity changes without substantial changes in movement velocity or smoothness: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00213-026-07106-8
why_it_matters: Directly examines hand coordination during drug exposure and cautions against equating plasticity with better dexterity or safe unsupervised exercise.
evidence_level: Phase 1 randomized dose-order study, 13 healthy adults; overlapping subset analysis, not two independent cohorts
date_note: Main report published 2026-08-07. Companion hand analysis published 2026-06-17, using 11 participants for task performance and 10 for kinematics from the same parent project; its cited parent preprint DOI is 10.64898/2025.12.22.25342874.
limitation: Small, young healthy-adult sample, no placebo-only condition, exploratory outcomes and possible practice effects. Not pediatric, brain tumor, stroke or injury-recovery evidence. Reported research doses are not treatment instructions. This is published research, not a verified recruiting opportunity.
care_question: Has any controlled study demonstrated lasting hand-function gains in people with my actual diagnosis?

title: Psilocybin given before chemotherapy protected sensory nerves in mouse models, not yet proven in patients
source: Science; UT MD Anderson Cancer Center
quick_read: MD Anderson researchers found that psilocybin given before chemotherapy prevented peripheral nerve injury in mouse models. Sensory nerve endings and touch sensitivity were preserved across several chemotherapy drugs and repeated treatment cycles. The experiments linked protection to the movement of energy-producing mitochondria inside nerve fibers. They do not establish prevention in people or reversal of longstanding nerve damage.
summary: Heles and colleagues studied platinum- and taxane-related neuropathy. Pretreatment preserved nerve endings and mitochondrial trafficking without reducing antitumor effects in the tested models. Institutional publication record with original abstract: https://mdanderson.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/psilocybin-prevents-chemotherapy-induced-peripheral-neuropathy-th/ . Official explanation: https://www.mdanderson.org/newsroom/research-newsroom/psilocybin-prevents-chemotherapy-related-nerve-injury-and-associated-symptoms-in-preclinical-models.h00-159858501.html
why_it_matters: A distinct nerve-protection research direction for chemotherapy-related sensory injury. It is not evidence for tumor-pressure-related hand weakness, clenching or traumatic nerve reconstruction.
evidence_level: Peer-reviewed preclinical mouse research; human preventive benefit unproven
date_note: Science publication date 2026-09-03, confirmed by the institutional publication record and original abstract.
limitation: Prevention before chemotherapy differs from treating established neuropathy or restoring motor function. Clinical safety, efficacy and individual eligibility are not established by these experiments. Full Science text was blocked; selected claims were verified in the original abstract and official institutional report. No recruitment claim is made.
care_question: Is the problem chemotherapy-related sensory neuropathy, or a different neurological impairment requiring another assessment route?

title: MDMA-assisted therapy reduced PTSD symptoms more than therapy with placebo in a phase 3 trial
quick_read: A randomized study of 104 adults with moderate to severe PTSD found greater symptom improvement with MDMA-assisted therapy than identical therapy with placebo. Both groups received psychological support. This is a positive mental-health result, not evidence of repairing nerves or restoring hand movement.
summary: The primary PTSD severity score fell by an estimated 23.7 points with MDMA plus therapy versus 14.8 with placebo plus therapy (p<0.001). The secondary disability measure also favored MDMA. Severe treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in five MDMA participants and two controls; no serious treatment-emergent events or deaths were reported.
why_it_matters: Adds human evidence for psychological recovery, distinct from motor rehabilitation.
evidence_level: Randomized, double-blind phase 3 trial; 104 adults; psychological outcomes
date_note: Background research, published 2023-09-14. Author-list correction dated 2024-10-07: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-024-03331-w
limitation: Expectancy and difficulty maintaining blinding limit interpretation. Not tumor, pediatric or motor-recovery evidence. MDMA remains unapproved for clinical use by the FDA, per the VA page checked 2026-10-25: https://www.ptsd.va.gov/understand_tx/mdma_assisted_therapy.asp .
care_question: What evidence-based support addresses psychological symptoms alongside neurological rehabilitation?

trial_status.status: Completed, checked 2026-10-25; registry last update posted 2025-06-06.
trial_status.location: Multisite study; see registry for historical locations.
trial_status.key_eligibility: Historical eligibility: adults 18 or older with PTSD. Exclusions included uncontrolled hypertension, significant cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, specified rhythm risks, symptomatic liver disease, pregnancy/nursing and active illicit or prescription drug use disorder. Full criteria apply; this completed study is not accepting new participants.

title: MDMA reopened a social-learning window in adult mice in an early brain-plasticity study
quick_read: A mouse study found that MDMA restored an adult brain's ability to learn from social reward. This ability is normally strongest during a limited developmental window. The result helped establish a research direction on reopening learning windows, but it did not test hand or walking recovery.
summary: Nardou and colleagues linked MDMA-induced reopening to oxytocin receptors in the nucleus accumbens, a reward-related brain region. Experiments showed changes in oxytocin-dependent synaptic plasticity alongside restored social reward learning.
why_it_matters: A mechanistic foundation for investigating drugs paired with structured learning, without assuming that social learning predicts motor recovery.
evidence_level: Controlled mouse behavioral and synaptic experiments; no human rehabilitation outcomes
date_note: Background research published 2019-04-03; added 2026-10-25. This is the original MDMA study, not a new clinical success or an additional human trial.
limitation: One type of learning in mice does not establish general brain rejuvenation, nerve repair or benefit after brain tumors. No human safety or clinical eligibility is established.
care_question: Has a proposed plasticity effect translated into meaningful function in people with the relevant condition?

title: Small MDMA-assisted therapy study reported substantial depression improvement, with controlled trials still needed
source: The British Journal of Psychiatry (Østfold Hospital Trust)
quick_read: Twelve adults with moderate to severe major depression received MDMA-assisted psychotherapy in a Norwegian study. Depression scores improved after treatment. Everyone received the intervention, so the study cannot separate drug effects from psychotherapy, expectations or natural improvement. This is an encouraging early signal rather than proof of effectiveness.
summary: Participants received two MDMA sessions a month apart with surrounding psychotherapy. Mean depression severity fell from 29.6 to 9.7 on the MADRS scale eight weeks after the second session; functional impairment also improved. No unexpected or serious adverse events were reported, although transient increases in blood pressure, heart rate and temperature occurred.
why_it_matters: Direct depression research, rather than assuming PTSD results apply to a different diagnosis.
evidence_level: Open-label uncontrolled study; 12 adults; preliminary safety and feasibility evidence
date_note: Background research published online 2025-07-11. Registered as EudraCT 2021-000805-26; the paper describes historical recruitment during 2023–2024, not a current opening.
limitation: No placebo or comparison group. Not evidence for brain tumor recovery, hand control or nerve regrowth. Not a pediatric study or established depression treatment.
care_question: What controlled evidence and supervised research options exist for the actual depression diagnosis?

title: Recruiting in Toronto: MDMA-assisted therapy pilot for severe chronic neuropathic pain
quick_read: EASE Pain is a Toronto pilot testing MDMA-assisted therapy for severe chronic neuropathic pain. It compares MDMA with methylphenidate as an active control, with psychological support in both groups. The main purpose is to determine whether a larger trial is feasible; pain and daily-function outcomes are also measured. No results are posted, and it is not a study of restoring hand movement or regrowing nerves.
summary: NCT07301632 plans 50 adults at St. Michael's Hospital, sponsored by Unity Health Toronto. The randomized, blinded phase 2 pilot includes preparation, one dosing session and integration sessions across a 16-week participant schedule. Primary outcomes concern feasibility, retention, data completion, blinding and adverse events. Clinical measures include pain interference, physical function, depression and anxiety. Published research contact: Akash Goel, MD, MPH, FRCPC; Akash.Goel@unityhealth.to; 416-864-5071. No contact has been made.
why_it_matters: A legitimate nerve-pain research route when clinically confirmed neuropathic pain is the problem. Sensory loss, clenching or weakness without qualifying pain does not establish a match.
evidence_level: Recruiting randomized, blinded, active-controlled phase 2 feasibility pilot; no results posted

trial_status.status: Recruiting in registry and at the St. Michael's Hospital site, rechecked on ClinicalTrials.gov 2026-10-25. Last update posted 2026-07-29; sponsor status-verification field remains October 2025.
trial_status.location: St. Michael's Hospital, Toronto, Ontario, Canada
trial_status.key_eligibility: Adults 18 or older with clinician-confirmed neuropathic pain longer than three months, specified moderate-to-severe pain thresholds, and inadequate benefit from at least two guideline-recommended medications; sufficient English for psychotherapy. Excludes seizure disorders, prior MDMA use, certain psychiatric conditions, pregnancy/breastfeeding, significant cardiovascular or organ disease, recent stroke/brain hemorrhage and numerous interacting medicines, including current SSRIs/SNRIs and specified anticonvulsants. Current psychotherapy specifically for chronic neuropathic pain is excluded. No upper time-since-injury limit or specific brain-tumor recovery indication is stated. The registry does not restrict neuropathic pain to peripheral-nerve causes; diagnosis must be made by a clinician trained in chronic pain and confirmed with the LANSS questionnaire. Full registry and individual study-team screening apply.

date_note: Background trial listing: first posted 2025-12-24, last update posted 2026-07-29. No benefit result is implied by recruitment status.
limitation: Not a depression-primary, brain-tumor hand rehabilitation or nerve-reconstruction trial. Trial listing does not confirm current spaces, travel eligibility or individual suitability. Do not stop prescribed medicines to try to qualify; ask the study team and treating clinician.
care_question: Is the pain clinically neuropathic, and do its severity, treatment history and current medicines permit screening?

title: Randomized trial in children after posterior fossa tumors: added coordination training improved upper-limb coordination scores
source: Journal of Cancer Research and Clinical Oncology (Cairo University; Children's Cancer Hospital Egypt 57357)
quick_read: Children treated for tumors at the back of the brain (posterior fossa) often have trouble with balance and coordination. In this Egyptian trial, 60 children aged 5 to 12 were randomly assigned to a core exercise program alone, or the same program plus balance training or plus coordination training. After 12 weeks, the coordination group scored higher than the core-only group on tests of two-handed and upper-limb coordination, and the balance group did better on balance tests. The study was small, single-center, and did not report side effects or how much each child improved from baseline.
summary: A three-arm randomized controlled trial (registered NCT04528316) enrolled 60 children aged 5 to 12 in the maintenance phase of posterior fossa tumor treatment at Children's Cancer Hospital Egypt 57357. All groups did Pilates-based core stability exercise (60 minutes per session); one group added 30 minutes of HUMAC balance and tilt training and another added 30 minutes of BOT-2 based coordination exercises. At week 12, the coordination group had higher BOT-2 upper-limb coordination (median 36 vs 25, p<0.0001) and bilateral coordination (22 vs 18, p<0.0001) scores than controls. The balance group outperformed controls on nearly all postural stability measures and also scored higher on upper-limb coordination (30 vs 25, p=0.005). Coordination training did not clearly improve postural measures. Only post-treatment medians are reported, session frequency is not stated, and adverse events are not reported.
why_it_matters: It is one of the few randomized trials in children with brain tumors that measured arm and hand coordination as a target of therapy. It suggests task-specific coordination practice improves coordination test scores more than general core exercise, though it does not measure everyday hand use, grasp or release.
relevance_reason: Randomized pediatric brain tumor trial with an upper-limb coordination outcome.
evidence_level: Human trial (randomized, three parallel groups, 60 children, single center)
date_note: Background research: published online 2022-12-16 (print 2023, volume 149). Older than 2024, included because tumor-specific arm coordination trials are rare. Registry NCT04528316 lists the study as completed (ages 5 to 12, checked 2026-10-25).
limitation: Single center; active comparison group; tumor subtypes, dose and adverse events not reported; outcomes are test scores at 12 weeks only, with no long-term follow-up or measure of daily hand use.
care_question: Would a coordination-focused program (not only general exercise or balance work) be appropriate for my child's arm and hand difficulties after posterior fossa tumor treatment?

title: Systematic review of outpatient rehabilitation after childhood brain tumors: function improved most often, but evidence is thin
source: Frontiers in Rehabilitation Sciences (University of Nottingham, Children's Brain Tumour Research Centre)
quick_read: Researchers in Nottingham pulled together 8 studies of outpatient rehabilitation for people who had a brain tumor in childhood. Physical therapy approaches, including intensive affected-arm training, balance and coordination programs, and video gaming, were the most common. Functional outcomes such as motor skills, balance and daily activities improved most often, but one gaming study found no gain in hand or manual coordination. The studies were small and short, so the authors say no firm conclusions can be drawn about which approach works best.
summary: This PROSPERO-registered systematic review (searches through November 2024) included 8 studies of 9 to 60 participants with childhood brain tumors, mostly randomized trials plus one quasi-experimental study and one case series. Interventions included constraint-induced movement therapy, dual-task and balance/coordination training, active video gaming, cognitive/academic programs, a problem-solving program and musical instrument training. Functional outcomes showed the most frequent significant improvements; arm-relevant findings included gains in motor skills and daily activities after constraint-induced therapy in a 9-child uncontrolled study, upper-limb coordination gains in a 60-child posterior fossa trial, and no significant change in manual or fine manual coordination with video gaming (13 children). Psychological and quality-of-life results were mixed, and fatigue and sleep were never assessed. Synthesis used vote counting because about 50 different outcome scales were used.
why_it_matters: It is a recent, structured overview of what has actually been tested for function after childhood brain tumors, including hand and arm approaches, and it makes clear how limited and mixed the evidence still is.
relevance_reason: Brain-tumor-specific review that includes upper-limb and hand-coordination outcomes in children.
evidence_level: Systematic review (8 small studies, high risk of bias in several, no meta-analysis)
date_note: Published 2026-06-01. Includes studies already listed separately on this site (for example the 2017 pediatric constraint-induced therapy pilot); the review itself is new.
limitation: Small, heterogeneous studies; short follow-up; vote-counting synthesis cannot estimate effect sizes; English-language only; some internal inconsistencies noted in the review's reporting.
care_question: Which of these rehabilitation approaches fits my child's specific problems (arm use, coordination, balance), and how will progress be measured?

title: About two in three people with eye-movement nerve palsy from skull base tumors improved, with earlier treatment linked to recovery
source: PLOS ONE (Asan Medical Center, University of Ulsan, Seoul)
quick_read: Tumors at the base of the skull can damage the nerves that move the eyes, causing double vision or an eye that turns in or out. This Seoul study reviewed 56 adults with third or sixth nerve palsy from such tumors. About two thirds improved by at least one grade, and those treated sooner after symptoms began were more likely to recover. Pituitary tumors recovered most often, while palsies from meningiomas often persisted. The study did not look at glasses with prisms, eye muscle surgery or similar eye treatments.
summary: A single-center retrospective cohort included 56 adults with MRI-confirmed third, fourth or sixth cranial nerve palsy due to primary skull base tumors (meningioma 23, pituitary adenoma 17, chordoma 7, others) with at least 6 months of follow-up. Recovery, defined as at least one grade of improvement without worsening, occurred in 37 of 56 (66.1%), with 33 reaching normal function; 7 worsened. A shorter interval from symptoms to treatment was associated with recovery (p=0.001). Pituitary adenoma palsies recovered in 15 of 17 (88.2%), while 13 of 23 meningioma palsies persisted or worsened. Patients in the non-recovery group had mostly received radiosurgery or radiotherapy rather than surgery, but treatment was not randomized. The abstract and discussion quote slightly different recovery percentages from the results table.
why_it_matters: It gives realistic expectations for eye turning and double vision caused by tumor-related nerve palsy and suggests the timing of tumor treatment matters. It describes tumor treatment, not eye-specific rehabilitation.
relevance_reason: Brain-tumor population with vision/eye-alignment outcomes (cranial nerve palsy).
evidence_level: Human study (retrospective cohort, 56 adults, single center, no multivariable analysis)
date_note: Background research: published 2024-08-29.
limitation: Retrospective; small groups per tumor type; treatment chosen clinically so comparisons between surgery and radiation may be confounded; inconsistent percentages within the paper; adult skull base tumors only.
care_question: Given my tumor type and how long the eye-movement problem has lasted, what are the chances it improves, and when should an orthoptist or strabismus specialist be involved?

title: Eye muscle surgery straightened eye alignment in most people with nerve palsy, a third of whom had brain tumors
source: Journal of Clinical Medicine (Medical University of Vienna)
quick_read: When a nerve that moves the eye is damaged, the eye can drift inward, outward or up and down, causing double vision. This Vienna study looked back at 57 people who had eye muscle (strabismus) surgery for such palsies; brain tumors were the single most common known cause, in 19 people. After surgery, about 81% had their eye misalignment reduced to 10 degrees or less. Sixth nerve palsies did best and third nerve palsies worst, and eight people needed another operation. Double vision itself was not measured.
summary: A retrospective single-center review (2009 to 2023) of 57 patients undergoing strabismus surgery for third, fourth, sixth or combined cranial nerve palsy. Causes included brain neoplasm in 19 (33% of all patients), vascular disease 14, trauma 13 and others. Success, defined as a postoperative angle of deviation of 10 degrees or less, was achieved in 46 of 57 (80.7%): 90% for isolated sixth nerve palsy, 87.5% for fourth, 71.4% for combined and 58.3% for third nerve palsy. Mean horizontal deviation fell from about 17 to 7 degrees at near and distance (p<0.001); vertical deviation did not change significantly overall. Eight reoperations were needed. No predictor, including cause, was significantly associated with success. Mean follow-up was about 11 months.
why_it_matters: For people left with a persistent eye turn after a brain tumor or its treatment, it shows that eye muscle surgery can often improve alignment, while being clear that third nerve palsies are harder to correct.
relevance_reason: Eye-alignment treatment in a mixed population where brain tumor was the most common cause; not tumor-only.
evidence_level: Human study (retrospective case series, 57 patients, single center)
date_note: Published 2025-10-13.
limitation: Mixed causes, with no outcomes reported separately for tumor patients; alignment-only success definition; no double vision or quality-of-life measures; short and variable follow-up.
care_question: Has my eye alignment been stable long enough to consider strabismus surgery, and which nerve is involved?

title: Review of headache after brain surgery: common, sometimes long-lasting, with few treatment trials so far
source: Current Pain and Headache Reports (Weill Cornell Medicine)
quick_read: Headache after a craniotomy is common, and in some people it continues for months. This review from Weill Cornell summarizes how often it happens, who is at higher risk, and which treatments have been tried. Scalp nerve blocks during surgery reduce pain in the first day, while longer-term options such as botulinum toxin injections and neck nerve blocks are supported only by small case series and observational studies. There are no clinical trials designed specifically for persistent post-craniotomy headache. This is about pain, not about movement or nerve recovery.
summary: A narrative review focused on 2021 to 2026 literature. It cites headache in roughly 60 to 70% of craniotomy patients, with about a quarter developing persistent headache, and quotes a 17% rate after tumor resection in one series (higher after microvascular decompression and suboccipital approaches). Risk factors include younger age, female sex, prior headache, muscle dissection and longer surgery. Intraoperative scalp blocks have moderate evidence for reducing early pain and analgesic use. For persistent headache, evidence is weak: drugs such as tricyclics and antiseizure medicines are supported mainly by anecdote; botulinum toxin case reports and series total 21 patients, 6 of whom became pain-free; two observational studies support cervical nerve blocks for neck-related headache. The authors stress small retrospective studies, inconsistent definitions and a lack of headache-specific trials.
why_it_matters: It gives a current, practical map of what is known about chronic head pain after brain surgery, including tumor surgery, and shows where evidence is still missing.
relevance_reason: Covers chronic post-craniotomy pain, which applies to many brain tumor survivors; not tumor-specific.
evidence_level: Narrative review (no formal evidence grading; underlying studies mostly small and observational)
date_note: Published 2026-08-05 (volume 30, article 103).
limitation: Narrative review rather than systematic; brain tumor patients are not analyzed separately; treatment evidence for persistent headache is low quality.
care_question: Is my ongoing head pain after surgery a recognized post-craniotomy headache type, and would a headache or pain specialist consider nerve blocks or other options?

title: Case report: botulinum toxin injections eased painful arm and leg stiffness in a teenager with an advanced brainstem tumor
source: Clinical Medicine Insights: Case Reports (Nara Prefectural General Medical Center, Japan)
quick_read: A 15-year-old with a recurrent tumor in the brainstem (pons) developed painful muscle stiffness (spasticity) in her arms and legs. Doctors injected botulinum toxin into stiff muscles in the upper arm, forearm flexors, thigh and lower leg over three sessions. Her pain score fell from 7.5 to 1 out of 10 and stayed low for months, and therapists reported easier stretching and more time for movement practice. This is a single case in a very advanced illness; it shows pain relief, not recovery of hand function.
summary: Single case report of a 15-year-old with diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma who, about three years after radiotherapy, developed recurrent tumor with painful spasticity (Modified Ashworth 3) in the upper and lower limbs. She declined opioid-type analgesics because of breathing concerns. Intramuscular botulinum toxin was given in three sessions (upper arm and thigh first, then forearm flexors and lower leg added; body text reports 200, 400 and 500 units, while the abstract lists different doses). Pain fell from NRS 7.5 to 1.0 and SF-MPQ-2 from 119 to 19 after the third session, with no injection-related adverse events reported. Passive range of motion became quicker to achieve. No hand-specific function, post-treatment spasticity score or caregiving measures were reported. She died at 27 weeks of disease-related respiratory failure. Concurrent bevacizumab, radiotherapy and other medicines may have contributed to the pain change.
why_it_matters: Spasticity in the arm after a brain tumor can be painful, and this case shows botulinum toxin, an established spasticity treatment, being used for tumor-related arm stiffness and pain. It should be read as pain and stiffness management, not as evidence of regained grasp or dexterity.
relevance_reason: Brain tumor patient with upper-limb spasticity (forearm flexors injected); outcome is pain, not hand function.
evidence_level: Case report (one patient)
date_note: Published online 2025-01-04.
limitation: Single advanced-stage case; confounding treatments; internal inconsistencies in reported doses and scores; no hand function or spasticity outcome after treatment.
care_question: Is arm or hand stiffness part of my symptoms, and would a spasticity assessment (including whether botulinum toxin could help comfort, positioning or hand opening) be appropriate?

title: Houston study of 130 glioma surgeries near movement areas: lasting new weakness in about 5%, with awake and asleep mapping similar
quick_read: Removing a glioma next to the brain's movement strip risks causing weakness, so surgeons map movement areas during the operation, either with the patient awake or under anesthesia. This Houston study reviewed 130 adults operated on between 2008 and 2024. About 5% had new or worse weakness still present at three months, with similar rates for awake and asleep mapping. Tumor removal amounts were also similar. The study did not report hand-specific outcomes or graded strength.
summary: A retrospective single-institution cohort of 130 adults with diffuse glioma in peri-Rolandic (motor/sensory cortex) regions, resected with awake (54) or asleep (76) motor mapping. New or worsened motor deficits persisting at 3 months occurred in 7 of 130 (5.4%): 5.6% awake vs 5.3% asleep (p=1.0). All persistent deficits occurred in glioblastoma patients; none in IDH-mutant tumors. Median extent of resection was about 95 to 98% in both groups, and mapping type did not predict extent of resection after adjusting for tumor volume. Glioblastoma survival did not differ significantly. Early postoperative deficit rates, hand-specific results and graded strength were not reported, and the groups differed at baseline (asleep patients were older with lower performance status).
why_it_matters: It gives a current estimate of how often surgery near the motor strip leaves lasting weakness when mapping is used, helpful context for people facing or recovering from this surgery.
relevance_reason: Brain tumor motor outcomes after surgery near motor cortex; no hand-specific data.
evidence_level: Human study (retrospective cohort, 130 patients, non-randomized)
date_note: Published online 2026-07-13 (volume 178, article 100).
limitation: Retrospective and non-randomized with baseline imbalances; small subgroups; no early-deficit, hand-specific or strength-grade data; some denominators unclear.
care_question: Was mapping used in my surgery, and does my current weakness fit the temporary or lasting pattern described in studies like this?

title: Seven inpatients after brain tumor surgery tried EEG neurofeedback alongside rehab, with improvements but no comparison group
source: Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback (ICS Maugeri IRCCS, Bari, Italy)
quick_read: Neurofeedback uses real-time brain wave (EEG) readings to train people to shift their own brain activity. In this Italian rehabilitation unit, seven adults recovering from surgery for meningiomas or a glioma did 15 neurofeedback sessions over three weeks on top of usual physical and occupational therapy. All seven showed reliable gains on memory, thinking or language tests, and daily independence scores improved. Without a comparison group, it is impossible to tell how much came from neurofeedback rather than usual rehab and natural recovery.
summary: Prospective case series of 7 consecutive inpatients (aged 46 to 76; six meningiomas, one glioma) after tumor resection. Each received 15 sessions of 35 minutes of individualized EEG neurofeedback (theta/beta or SMR/theta protocols at sites chosen from lesion location and quantitative EEG) five days a week, plus about one hour daily of conventional motor rehabilitation and occupational training. Reliable change was reported in cognitive measures for all participants and in FIM and Modified Barthel scores for most. No hand or upper-limb specific measure was used. No adverse events occurred. The authors list no control group, no correction for multiple comparisons, heterogeneity and no follow-up after discharge as key limitations.
why_it_matters: It is one of very few reports of neurofeedback specifically in brain tumor rehabilitation, so it flags a feasible add-on worth proper trials. It does not show that neurofeedback restores arm or hand movement.
relevance_reason: Brain tumor population; general function and cognition outcomes, no hand data.
evidence_level: Human study (uncontrolled case series, 7 patients)
date_note: Published online 2025-11-04 (print 2026, volume 51, issue 2).
limitation: Tiny uncontrolled series; concurrent rehabilitation and spontaneous recovery cannot be separated; no hand outcomes; no follow-up.
care_question: Is neurofeedback offered in a research setting near me, and would it replace or only add to standard rehabilitation?

title: Pilot trial: implanted vagus nerve stimulation paired with arm therapy was feasible in chronic neck spinal cord injury
source: Frontiers in Rehabilitation Sciences (UTHealth Houston and TIRR Memorial Hermann)
quick_read: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) gives brief pulses through an implanted device in the neck while a person practices movements, aiming to strengthen the brain and spinal pathways being used. In this Houston pilot, six adults with long-standing incomplete spinal cord injury in the neck received either real or sham stimulation during 18 arm and hand therapy sessions plus home exercise. There were no serious complications, and all three people with real stimulation improved on a hand and arm test right after therapy, two of them meaningfully at 90 days. With only six people, these results are a safety and feasibility signal, not proof that it works. This is a spinal cord injury study and does not apply directly to brain tumor or nerve injuries.
summary: Single-site, triple-blind, sham-controlled pilot RCT (NCT05601661) in 6 adults with chronic traumatic incomplete cervical SCI (AIS B to D, C3 to C5, 16 to 61 months after injury). All were implanted with the Vivistim system and randomized 1:1 to active VNS (0.8 mA, paired with movement attempts) or 0 mA sham during 18 in-clinic 90-minute sessions over 6 to 8 weeks, followed by a 90-day home program. No serious adverse events or unresolved device complications occurred; cough during stimulation and mild neck pain were reported. Four of six completed all sessions; home adherence averaged 59%. Exploratory GRASSP scores of the trained arm improved in all three active participants immediately after therapy and in none of the sham participants; at 90 days two active participants met a 6-point threshold. Results were descriptive only, and enrollment stopped at six for budget reasons.
why_it_matters: It extends paired VNS, already approved for arm rehabilitation after stroke, into spinal cord injury with a sham control, keeping the spinal cord evidence distinct from brain and peripheral nerve injury.
relevance_reason: Post-accident arm and hand recovery after cervical spinal cord injury (priority 3, spinal cord category).
evidence_level: Human trial (pilot randomized, sham-controlled, 6 participants; exploratory efficacy)
date_note: Published online 2026-05-22; final version 2026-06-11. Registry NCT05601661 lists the study as completed (checked 2026-10-25); it is not a recruitment opportunity.
limitation: Six participants; descriptive analysis only; baseline heterogeneity; some participants received spasticity injections; reporting inconsistencies in adverse-event percentages.
care_question: For neck spinal cord injury, are there larger paired VNS studies I could be screened for, and what surgery and therapy commitment does it involve?

title: Small Brazilian series: extra nerve transfer to a shoulder-rotating muscle gave useful outward rotation after upper brachial plexus injury
source: Brain & Spine (University of Sao Paulo Medical School)
quick_read: Injuries to the upper part of the brachial plexus (the C5 and C6 nerve roots) make it hard to lift the arm and turn it outward. Surgeons in Sao Paulo added a transfer of a small nerve branch from the triceps directly to the infraspinatus, a muscle that rotates the shoulder outward, alongside other standard transfers. Seven adults were followed for a median of almost five years, and five reached at least 45 degrees of outward rotation, with no complications reported. This is a peripheral nerve study, separate from spinal cord or brain injury, and too small to prove the extra transfer is better.
summary: Retrospective case series from the University of Sao Paulo. Of 11 consecutive adults with complete C5/C6 brachial plexus lesions operated within a year of injury (mean 6.5 months), 7 were evaluable (one died of cancer, three lost to follow-up). In addition to ulnar fascicle to biceps, medial pectoral to axillary and spinal accessory to suprascapular transfers, a radial branch to the triceps was transferred directly to the infraspinatus branch. At median 4.7 years, mean external rotation was 62 degrees (95% CI 37 to 86), with 5 of 7 reaching the authors' 45-degree good-result threshold. Recovery began after 4 months, once as late as month 14. Comparisons with the authors' unpublished historical data are not independently validated. Cause of injury was not stated and strength was not reported.
why_it_matters: Shoulder outward rotation is often weak after upper plexus repair; this adds long-term follow-up for one technique aimed at that specific gap, clearly within the peripheral nerve (not spinal cord or brain) category.
relevance_reason: Post-injury arm dysfunction from brachial plexus (peripheral nerve) injury.
evidence_level: Human study (retrospective case series, 7 evaluated patients, no control group)
date_note: Published 2026-06-10 (Brain & Spine volume 6, article 106114).
limitation: Very small, uncontrolled, with substantial loss to follow-up; non-standard success threshold; injury mechanism and strength not reported.
care_question: After a brachial plexus injury, which nerve transfers are being considered for shoulder rotation, and what is the timing window for surgery?

title: Johns Hopkins recruiting a small Phase 1 psilocybin safety study in chronic stroke, with arm function as a secondary measure
quick_read: Johns Hopkins is testing whether psilocybin, the active compound in 'magic mushrooms', is safe for people at least a year after a stroke. About 20 adults will receive either a single 25 mg dose or two 12.5 mg doses two hours apart, with blood pressure stability as the main measure. Arm and hand tests are collected as secondary measures, but the study is not designed to show whether movement improves. It is for stroke only, not brain tumors, and many common medicines (including several antidepressants and seizure medicines) exclude people.
summary: NCT07053917 (PHATHOM) is an open-label Phase 1 study at Johns Hopkins, Baltimore, with a target of 20 adults with CT- or MRI-confirmed ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke at least 12 months earlier. Two psilocybin regimens (Usona Institute product) are compared: 25 mg once, or 12.5 mg followed by 12.5 mg two hours later. The primary outcome is blood pressure staying within set limits for 24 hours after dosing; motor outcomes reported in the listing include the Fugl-Meyer upper extremity, ARAT and nine-hole peg test. Exclusions include recent use of SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, bupropion, lithium, trazodone and several anticonvulsants, psychosis or bipolar I history, suicidality, substance use disorders, and neurological conditions that interfere with motor assessment. The listing does not describe a paired rehabilitation program. Start date 2026-02-09; primary completion estimated 2027-02-01.
why_it_matters: It is the first registered human study we found that collects arm and hand measures after psilocybin in people with brain injury, following animal plasticity research. It is a safety study in stroke and says nothing yet about recovery, and stroke findings should not be assumed to apply to brain tumors.
relevance_reason: Genuinely new experimental psilocybin trial with upper-limb measures; stroke only, not tumor.
evidence_level: Recruiting Phase 1 open-label safety study; 20 planned; no results

trial_status.status: Recruiting in registry and at the Johns Hopkins site, checked on ClinicalTrials.gov 2026-10-25. Last update posted 2026-02-13; status verified February 2026. No results posted.
trial_status.key_eligibility: Adults over 18 with ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke confirmed by CT or MRI at least 12 months earlier; English speaking; consent to recorded sessions. Excludes recent serotonergic antidepressants, lithium, trazodone and several anticonvulsants, psychosis or bipolar I history, suicidality, substance use disorder, uncontrolled blood pressure or cardiac problems, weight under 48 kg, pregnancy, and conditions interfering with motor assessment. Brain tumor is not a listed condition.

date_note: Registry first posted 2025-07-08; study start 2026-02-09; last update posted 2026-02-13. Checked directly on ClinicalTrials.gov 2026-10-25.
